newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader pushes on with referendum campaign.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader pushes on with referendum campaign.

text.p: Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko was on collision course with parliament on Thursday after refusing to scrap a referendum on extending his powers.

An aide said Lukashenko would take his referendum campaign to Brest, 350 km (200 miles) west of Minsk on the Polish border, after renewing his pledge to push ahead with Sunday's referendum and snubbing mediation efforts by Russia.

His rival, parliament chairman Semyon Sharetsky, met Russian mediators on Wednesday. But the constitutional court kept tensions high by saying it would convene on Friday to hear an impeachment case lodged against Lukashenko by parliament.
Yegor Stroyev, the chairman of Russia's upper house of parliament, voiced his concern over the crisis after meeting Sharetsky in the western Russian city of Smolensk.

"We reached a unanimous opinion that any further deepening of the conflict between the two branches of power in Belarus would bring the Belarussian people nothing but division, tragedy and trouble," he said after 90 minutes of talks.

The talks in Smolensk produced signs that the Belarus parliament would be ready to compromise over some of Lukashenko's planned constitutional changes provided the president also offered to compromise.

Sharetsky said before the talks that parliament wanted Lukashenko to cancel the referendum, withdraw his proposed constitutional changes and a series of illegal decrees, reinstate the sacked head of the Central Electoral Commission and give deputies television time.

But hopes of a major breakthrough were dashed by Lukashenko's refusal to attend the talks. One of his aides said he had not gone because Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin had decided not to attend.

Lukashenko later said in an interview with the Russian news agency Interfax that the parliamentarians must halt their impeachment moves if they want compromise. He said he had made repeated efforts at reconciliation but they had been ignored.

Lukashenko, 42, has been under fire from Western leaders and neighbouring countries over his plans to increase his term as president by more than two years and extend his powers over all institutions in Belarus.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin, urging compromise, spoke to him by telephone for 40 minutes on Wednesday.
But Lukashenko later renewed his pledge to hold the referendum, in which early voting began on November 9 in the country of 10 million people bordering Russia, Ukraine, Poland, Latvia and Lithuania.
"I will not give up the referendum. Thousands of people have already cast their votes. We will carry it to the end," he told electoral officials in Minsk.
Lukashenko aide Ural Latypov said Chernomyrdin might go to Belarus to meet Lukashenko on Friday or Saturday.
A Russian government official said in Moscow that no such trip featured in Chernomyrdin's plans and he was planning to visit Murmansk on Friday.

But Lukashenko said in an interview on Belarussian state television he might still meet Chernomyrdin soon. "If the situation becomes complicated, he (Chernomyrdin) may fly straight to Minsk from Murmansk," he said.
Asked what his concept of strong powers was, Lukashenko said he favoured "a new democratic life" and that "strong power must be in strong hands".
